newsitem.title: USA: Silver demand seen up on Clinton solar power plan.
newsitem.headline: Silver demand seen up on Clinton solar power plan.

text.p: The Clinton Administration's initiative, unveiled Friday, to expand the use of solar power, will help boost demand for silver, the Silver Institute said.
"The worldwide growth in demand for solar power provides another expanding market for silver," Silver Institute president Paul Bateman said.
"Silver's unique properties including electrical conductivity and sensitivity to light make it indispensable to this technology," he said.

U.S. President Clinton told the U.N. Earth Conference in New York Friday that the U.S. would work to reduce its reliance on fossil fuels by installing solar panels on one million more roofs around the nation by 2010.
U.S. Energy Secretary Federico Pena outlined details of the "Million Solar Roofs Initiative" Friday.
The state of Arizona and the city of Detroit, Michigan, recently introduced a solar energy program also.

Silver paste is used in 90 percent of all crystalline silicon photovoltaic cells, which are the most common solar cell, said Jeffrey Mazur, an engineer in the Photovoltaic Technology Division of the U.S. Energy Department.
All silicon cells used in the NASA space program to power satellites already use silver in the form of evaporated metal to make the electrical contact.
Sunlight striking the silicon cells generates electrons, which the silver conductors collect into an electric current.
The conductive silver is applied in the form of a glass paste with a minimum of 90 percent silver across the top and bottom of the silicon crystal.
A group of roofing-tile solar cells can generate enough power to supply a house and also fill batteries to supply power after dark, Mazur said.
The export of solar technology is growing at a rate of 15 to 18 percent a year, said John Thornton, an expert in photovoltaic markets at the National Renewable Energy Laboratory in Golden, Colorado.
